He worked hard to halt Protestantism's growth. Persecution, though, was not generally his policy. Hamilton's Catechism served his Catholic campaign in print. Protestants imprisoned him in 1563 once they held power. Released, he became an active partisan of Mary, queen of Scots. He baptised the infant James and pronounced Mary's divorce from Bothwell. After Langside he sheltered in Dumbarton Castle. Seized there, he was hanged on 6 April 1571. The charge was complicity in the Darnley and Murray murders.
britannica-1911-hampden-john:
John Hampden (c. 1595–1643) was an English statesman. He was born about 1595 at Great Hampden in Buckinghamshire. His mother was Oliver Cromwell's aunt. His father's early death left him a good estate. Thame grammar school and Magdalen College, Oxford, educated him. The Inner Temple admitted him in 1613. He first sat in Parliament in 1621 for Grampound. Wendover and Buckinghamshire returned him at later stages.

Popular imagination makes him the revolution's central early figure. His resistance to ship-money fixed that fame. Character explains the rest of it. He was massive yet modest, brave yet charitable. He shielded others from the costs of their actions. He let Eliot, then Pym, take the louder roles. His statue stands in St Stephen's Hall. It types the noblest parliamentary opposition. The long narrative ends by demolishing two beloved legends. His dying prayer and a famous portrait both prove forgeries.
britannica-1911-hancock-john:
John Hancock (1737–1793) was an American Revolutionary statesman. He was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, on 23 January 1737. Harvard graduated him in 1754. He entered his uncle Thomas Hancock's mercantile house in Boston. The uncle had adopted him. In 1764 he inherited a large fortune and the business. Boston made him a selectman in 1765. The general court took him the next year.

Customs officers seized his sloop Liberty in 1768. They charged unpaid duties on a cargo of Madeira. The suits against him failed but made him popular. His resentment of British government hardened. He presided over both Massachusetts Provincial Congresses. Gage's Lexington expedition aimed partly at capturing him and Adams. He presided over the Continental Congress from 1775 to 1777. He signed the Declaration of Independence first. Repeated election as governor proved his popularity. He died at Quincy in 1793.
britannica-1911-hawkesworth-john:
John Hawkesworth (c. 1715–1773) was an English miscellaneous writer. He was born in London about 1715. He may have clerked for an attorney. He was certainly self-educated. In 1744 he succeeded Johnson compiling parliamentary debates. The Gentleman's Magazine was his platform. With Johnson he started The Adventurer periodical. It ran to 140 numbers, half of them his. Canterbury rewarded his moral writing with an LL.D.

His twelve-volume Swift edition appeared in 1754–1755. A larger one ran to twenty-seven volumes. He adapted Dryden and Southerne for Drury Lane. His oriental tale Almoran and Hamet appeared in 1761. The admiralty commissioned him to edit Cook's first voyage papers. His three-volume Account appeared in 1773. Publishers reportedly paid him £6,000 for it. Critics attacked his South Seas descriptions as inexact. Their severity is said to have hastened his death.
britannica-1911-hawkshaw-sir-john:
Sir John Hawkshaw (1811–1891) was an English engineer born in Yorkshire. Leeds grammar school educated him. Six or seven years of railway and road work preceded his majority. In 1832 he became engineer to a mining association in Venezuela. The climate broke his health within two years. Liverpool docks employed him under Jesse Hartley on his return. The Manchester, Bury and Bolton Canal followed.

In 1845 he became chief engineer to the Manchester & Leeds railway. Its successor, the Lancashire & Yorkshire, kept him for decades. London practice began in 1850 as a consulting engineer. Charing Cross and Cannon Street railways were his work. Their Thames bridges came from him too. The East London railway runs through Brunel's tunnel under his charge. The Severn Tunnel ranks among the century's great undertakings. He died in London on 2 June 1891.
britannica-1911-hawkwood-sir-john:
Sir John Hawkwood (d. 1394) was an English adventurer in Italy. He won great wealth as a condottiere. Tradition makes him a tanner's son from Sibil Hedingham in Essex. He was apprenticed in London, then soldiered in France. Edward III and the Black Prince led that army. The peace of Bretigny in 1360 freed his company. He collected men-at-arms and moved south to Italy.

His White Company fought for Monferrato against Milan in 1362. Pisa, Florence, Perugia and the pope all hired him in turn. Resigning once over a council's interference showed his pride. Florence paid him 130,000 gold florins in 1375 for neutrality. A pension of 1,200 florins a year followed that bargain. In 1377 he massacred Cesena's inhabitants on a cardinal's orders. Disgust at executioner's work changed his allegiance within months. Temple-Leader's Giovanni Acuto tells his full story.
britannica-1911-hayward-sir-john:
Sir John Hayward (c. 1560–1627) was an English historian born near Felixstowe. Pembroke College, Cambridge, gave him degrees through the LL.D. In 1599 he published his Life and Raigne of King Henrie IV. He dedicated it to the earl of Essex. Elizabeth disliked the book and its dedication. She ordered Bacon to search it for treason. Bacon found none, but much felony, he joked. The sentences, he said, were stolen from Tacitus.

Hayward stayed in prison until about 1601 anyway. James I's accession let him court the new king. Pamphlets on succession and union followed in 1603. In 1610 he became a historiographer of James' Chelsea college. His Lives of the Three Norman Kings appeared in 1613. A knighthood came in 1619. His Edward VI was found among his manuscripts. It was first published in 1630, after his death.
britannica-1911-heathcoat-john:
John Heathcoat (1783–1861) was an English inventor born at Duffield. A framesmith's apprenticeship near Loughborough trained him. He improved the warp-loom to make lace-like mitts. Business at Nottingham drew competing inventors' intrusions. He removed to Hathern, then Loughborough. In 1808 he built a machine imitating real pillow-lace exactly. It was the most complex textile apparatus yet existing. He patented the invention in 1809.

Luddites attacked his Loughborough factory in 1816. They destroyed all 55 lace frames. Damages of £10,000 were assessed but never paid him. He rebuilt at once at Tiverton in Devon. Improved machines ran there by water, then steam. Rivals disputed his patent; a trial in 1816 upheld it. Parliament took him in later life for committee work. His business knowledge was highly valued there. He died near Tiverton in 1861.
britannica-1911-hely-hutchinson-john:
John Hely-Hutchinson (1724–1794) was an Irish lawyer and statesman. He was educated at Trinity College, Dublin. The Irish bar called him in 1748. His marriage in 1751 brought him the name Hutchinson. His wife was heiress to her uncle Richard Hutchinson. He entered the Irish Commons for Lanesborough in 1759. After 1761 he represented Cork city instead. He began with the patriotic opposition party.

Lord Townshend called him parliament's most powerful man. William Gerard Hamilton praised his ability and honesty. Yet he was an inveterate place-hunter too. Lord North joked he would ask the Isle of Man as a potato garden. He became secretary of state in 1777. In 1782 he read Portland's message on Irish independence. Grattan's triumph followed that same day. He supported parliamentary reform late in life. He died at Buxton on 4 September 1794. His wife had been created Baroness Donoughmore in 1785.
britannica-1911-henderson-john:
John Henderson (1747–1785) was an English actor of Scottish descent. He was born in London. His stage debut came at Bath on 6 October 1772. He played Hamlet on that first appearance. Success in Shakespeare earned him the nickname Bath Roscius. A London engagement proved hard to obtain. The Haymarket finally took him as Shylock in 1777. Colman profited considerably from that success.

Sheridan then engaged him for Drury Lane for two years. Covent Garden received him when the companies combined. He played Richard III there in 1778. He created original parts in plays by Cumberland and others. His last appearance was as Horatius in 1785. He died on 25 November that year. Westminster Abbey received his burial. Garrick was jealous of him, and mimicry estranged Colman. Gainsborough, Stewart and Romney all painted his portrait. He co-wrote a practical method for reading English poetry.
britannica-1911-heywood-john:
John Heywood (b. 1497) was an English dramatist and epigrammatist, said to be a native of North Mimms, near St Albans. He was a chorister of the Chapel Royal. From 1521 the king's accounts pay him ten marks a year as a player of the virginals. In 1538 he played an interlude with his children before the Princess Mary.

Heywood's wit and music made him a favourite with Henry VIII and with Mary. Sir Thomas More took an interest in him, and his Epigrams are tied to More's seat at Gobions. Under Edward VI he was charged with denying the king's supremacy and recanted in public in 1554. Under Mary he spoke at her coronation and won a manor lease in Yorkshire. When Elizabeth succeeded, he fled to Malines. By 1587 he is spoken of as dead and gone.
britannica-1911-hill-john:
John Hill (c. 1716–1775), styled Sir John Hill from his Swedish honours, was an English author, said to have been born in Peterborough. Apprenticed to an apothecary, he kept a small shop in Westminster and travelled hunting rare herbs. His first publication was a translation of Theophrastus's History of Stones (1746).

Hill then wrote without pause: magazines, a daily letter called The Inspector, novels, plays and science. His scurrilous attacks bred quarrels with Fielding, Smart and Garrick. From 1759 to 1775 he worked on The Vegetable System, 26 folio volumes with 1,600 engravings, for his patron Lord Bute. Sweden gave him the order of Vasa in 1774. He also grew rich as a quack doctor on vegetable medicines.
britannica-1911-hilton-john:
John Hilton (1804–1878) was a British surgeon, born at Castle Hedingham in Essex. He entered Guy's Hospital in 1824, became demonstrator of anatomy in 1828 and surgeon in 1849. In 1867 he was president of the Royal College of Surgeons and gave the Hunterian oration. His lectures on Rest and Pain (1859–1862) became classics.

Hilton was the greatest anatomist of his time, nicknamed Anatomical John. With the artist Joseph Towne he stocked Guy's with a unique collection of models. As an operator he was cautious rather than brilliant, though the method for opening deep abscesses bears his name. Yet he was the first to reduce an obturator hernia by abdominal section. He died at Clapham in 1878.
britannica-1911-holt-sir-john:
Sir John Holt (1642–1710) was lord chief justice of England, born at Thame, Oxfordshire, in 1642. His father, a lawyer of small success, became a serjeant and was knighted for Tory services. John entered Oriel College, Oxford, at sixteen, and is said to have spent a wild youth, even taking purses on the highway. At Gray's Inn from about 1660 he turned to diligent study, and was called to the bar in 1663.

Holt stood out in the state trials of the day for his bold defence of accused men, being an ardent friend of civil and religious liberty. He became recorder of London in 1685–1686 and king's sergeant, with a knighthood. A ruling against the king's claim to martial law in peacetime cost him the recordership. He helped arrange the settlement that called William III to the throne, and under William he became lord chief justice of the King's Bench.
britannica-1911-home-john:
John Home (1722–1808) was a Scottish dramatic poet, born at Leith on the 22nd of September 1722. His father was town-clerk there and distantly kin to the earls of Home. Home graduated at Edinburgh in 1742, studied divinity, and was licensed in 1745. That year he volunteered against the Pretender, was taken at Falkirk in 1746, and escaped from Doune castle. In July 1746 he was presented to the parish of Athelstaneford.

Home's first play, Agis, founded on Plutarch, was finished in 1747 and refused by Garrick for Drury Lane. His Douglas grew from hearing the ballad of Gil Morrice sung. After five years' labour he took it to London, where Garrick refused it too. Edinburgh staged it on the 14th of December 1756 to overwhelming success, against the presbytery's opposition. Home wisely resigned his charge in 1757.
britannica-1911-hotham-sir-john:
Sir John Hotham (d. 1645) was an English parliamentarian of a Yorkshire family. He fought on the continent in the early Thirty Years' War, was made a baronet in 1622, and sat for Beverley in the five parliaments between 1625 and 1640. He was sheriff of Yorkshire in 1635. In 1639 the king took from him the governorship of Hull, and he joined the parliamentary party, refusing ship-money.

In January 1642 parliament ordered Hotham to seize Hull, with its great store of munitions; his son John carried out the order. Hotham took command and in April 1642 refused to admit Charles I to the town. Later he promised his prisoner Lord Digby that he would give Hull up, yet when Charles came again he refused a second time and drove off the besiegers. His son, active in Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, soon fell out with the other parliamentary leaders.
britannica-1911-howard-john:
John Howard (1726–1790) was an English philanthropist and prison reformer, born at Hackney, probably on the 2nd of September 1726. His childhood passed at Cardington, near Bedford, where his father, a retired merchant, held a small estate. Apprenticed to London grocers, he bought up his indenture when his father died in 1742 and left him property. Travel followed, and weak health made him an invalid.

Nursed through a sharp illness by his landlady, a widow of fifty-three, Howard married her in 1752 out of gratitude; she died within three years. Sailing then for Portugal, he was taken by a French privateer, an early taste of captivity. As sheriff he turned to the prisons, finding men held for months over unpaid gaolers' fees. In 1777 his State of the Prisons in England and Wales laid the evils bare. He toured Europe's prisons for years, and died of camp fever at Kherson in January 1790.
britannica-1911-howe-john:
John Howe (1630–1706) was an English Puritan divine, born on the 17th of May 1630 at Loughborough, Leicestershire, where his father was vicar. He entered Christ's College, Cambridge, as a sizar in 1647 and took his B.A. the next year. There he knew Ralph Cudworth, Henry More and John Smith, and his mind took the Platonic tinge that marks his writings.

Howe moved to Oxford, becoming fellow and chaplain of Magdalen College, and took his M.A. in 1652. Ordained by Charles Herle, he went in 1654 as perpetual curate to Great Torrington in Devon. His preaching there grew into the treatises on The Blessedness of the Righteous, on which his fame rests. The long life follows him through the troubles of the Puritan clergy after the Restoration, and through the works that kept his name among the great nonconformist writers.
britannica-1911-kay-john:
John Kay (1742–1826) was a Scottish caricaturist, born near Dalkeith, where his father was a mason. At thirteen he was apprenticed to a barber and served him for six years. He then went to Edinburgh, where in 1771 he gained the freedom of the city by joining the corporation of barber surgeons.

In 1785, encouraged by the favour that met his first trials at etching, he took down his barber's pole and opened a small print shop in Parliament Square. There he thrived, painting miniatures and issuing at short gaps his sketches and caricatures of the local celebrities and oddities who filled Edinburgh society in that age. He died on the 21st of February 1826. His portraits were gathered by Hugh Paton and issued in 1838 as a series of original portraits and caricature etchings, a record held to be without match for its time and place.
britannica-1911-kempe-john:
John Kempe (c. 1380–1454) was an English cardinal, archbishop of Canterbury, and chancellor. He was the son of Thomas Kempe, a gentleman of Ollantigh near Ashford in Kent, and was born about 1380. He was trained at Merton College, Oxford, and practised as a church lawyer. He sat as an assessor at the trial of Oldcastle, and in 1415 became dean of the Court of Arches.

He then passed into royal service and worked in the government of Normandy, in time becoming chancellor of the duchy. Early in 1419 he was elected bishop of Rochester and consecrated at Rouen that December. He moved to Chichester in February 1421 and to London that November. In the minority of Henry VI he held a chief place in the council as a supporter of Henry Beaufort. He followed Beaufort as chancellor in March 1426, and that year he was raised to the archbishopric of York.
britannica-1911-ker-john:
John Ker (1673–1726) was a Scottish spy, born in Ayrshire on the 8th of August 1673. His true name was Crawfurd, and his father was Alexander Crawfurd of Crawfurdland. He married Anna, the younger daughter of Robert Ker of Kersland, whose only son had been killed at Steinkirk in 1692. In 1697, after buying the family estates from his wife's elder sister, he took the name and arms of Ker.

He became a leader among the extreme Covenanters and used his sway to ease his money troubles. He sold his support at one time to the Jacobites, at another to the government, and when he could to both at once. A government licence of 1707, letting him mix with men of known or suspected disloyalty, proves he was by then the government's paid spy. In his Memoirs Ker claims that he ran a ring of other spies besides.
britannica-1911-kirk-sir-john:
Sir John Kirk (1832– ) was a British naturalist and administrator, son of the Reverend John Kirk, born at Barry near Arbroath on the 19th of December 1832. After serving on the civil medical staff through the Crimean War, he was named in February 1858 physician and naturalist to David Livingstone's second expedition to Central Africa.

He was at Livingstone's side through most of his travels over the next five years. He was one of the first four white men to see Lake Nyassa, on the 16th of September 1859. At last, broken in health, he was sent home on the 9th of May 1863. The name he won on that expedition led to his appointment in January 1866 as acting surgeon to the political agency at Zanzibar. In 1868 he became assistant political agent, rising to consul general in 1873 and agent in 1880. He retired from that post in 1887.
britannica-1911-kirkby-john:
John Kirkby (d. 1290) was an English churchman and statesman. He entered the public service as a clerk of the chancery under Henry III. Under Edward I he acted as keeper of the great seal during the frequent absences of the chancellor, Robert Burnell, and was called vice chancellor.

In 1282 the king sent him through the counties and boroughs to gather money, and this and his other services were well rewarded. Though not yet ordained priest, he held several rich benefices in the church. In 1283 he was chosen bishop of Rochester, but the archbishop of Canterbury, John Peckham, opposed him, and he did not press his claim. In 1286, two years after he became treasurer, he was elected bishop of Ely. He was then ordained priest and consecrated by Peckham. He died at Ely on the 26th of March 1290, remembered as a benefactor to his see.
britannica-1911-knox-john:
John Knox (c. 1505–1572) was the Scottish reformer and historian at the centre of one of the longest life articles in this part of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Even his birth year is in doubt: the claims for 1505, 1513 and 1515 are weighed, and Knox himself said little of his early life. He was a son of William Knox, who lived in or near Haddington, was schooled there, and studied under the scholar John Major, first at Glasgow and then at St Andrews.

The article follows his rise as preacher and leader of the Scottish Reformation, and gives close study to his writings, above all his History of the Reformation. Church order takes up much of the later text: the pattern of ministers, elders, readers and superintendents, drawn from the Genevan church order under Calvin and from the German church in London. His letters are used throughout as a main source.
britannica-1911-kyrle-john:
John Kyrle (1637–1724), known as "the Man of Ross," was an English philanthropist, born in the parish of Dymock, Gloucestershire, on the 22nd of May 1637. His father was a barrister, and the family had lived at Ross in Herefordshire. Coming into the property at Ross, he settled there and gave his life to the good of the little town. He worked for the schooling of its children, alms for its poor, and the mending and adorning of the place itself.

Kyrle loved to make peace between neighbours who had quarrelled,. He was open-handed to the poor and spent all he had on good works, and he worked much in the open air beside the labourers on his farm. He died on the 7th of November 1724 and was buried in the chancel of Ross Church. The Kyrle Society, founded in 1877, keeps his name alive in work for working people.
britannica-1911-la-farge-john:
John La Farge (1835–1910) was an American artist, born in New York on the 31st of March 1835, of French parentage. His grandfather, a painter of miniatures, taught him drawing, and he studied law and architecture before entering the atelier of Thomas Couture in Paris. There he gave his care to the old masters at the Louvre. He began with illustrations to the poets. His closeness to the artist William M. Hunt, with whom he worked at Newport, Rhode Island, shaped him strongly.

From 1866 La Farge was for some years unfit for work. When his strength returned he did decorative work for Trinity church, Boston, in 1876, and turned to stained glass. He became president of the Society of Mural Painters. His commissions include windows for New York churches, the "Battle Window" in Memorial Hall at Harvard, panels for the Congressional Library at Washington, and work at the Capitol at St Paul.
britannica-1911-langton-john:
John Langton (died 1337) served England as chancellor. He ended as bishop of Chichester. A clerk in the royal chancery, he became chancellor in 1292. Church posts followed. Pope Boniface VIII blocked his bid for Ely in 1298. Edward I backed that bid. Langton even went to Rome for it.

He gave up the seal in 1302. Chichester came in 1305. He held the seal again under Edward II from 1307. The ordainers chose him in 1310. That link likely cost him office. Later he acted as go-between for the king. He served with Earl Thomas of Lancaster in 1318. He served again with rebel barons in 1321. He built the chapter house at Chichester.
britannica-1911-lesley-john:
John Lesley (1527-1596) was a Scottish bishop and historian. Aberdeen gave him his master's degree. A church post came to him in 1538 by special leave. He was a natural son, and the leave let him hold it all the same. Law study at Poitiers, Toulouse, and Paris made him a doctor in 1553. Orders came in 1558.

At the Reformation he stood firm for the old faith. He faced Knox in public debate at Edinburgh in 1561. That year he helped fetch Queen Mary home to rule. A privy council seat and a law chair at Aberdeen followed. In 1565 he became a judge and abbot of Lindores. The see of Ross came next, in 1565. He helped revise the laws of Scotland. The Black Acts were printed in 1566, much by his care. Mary kept his loyalty through her fall.
britannica-1911-locke-john:
John Locke's long 1911 article is held here in a middle chunk, and the hosted text opens deep in the thought, not at the life. Matter and its traits fill these pages. First traits — bulk, shape, count, place, and motion — stay in things whether seen or not. Second traits, such as colour and sound, live in our sense of things.

Four kinds of accord ground all claim to know. One kind is sameness or lack of it among ideas. One is math-like links. One is traits that sit or fail to sit in one thing. One is plain being, apart from our sight of it. Sight at once, proof by steps, and sense grasp form the three roads to truth. Sense grasp sits lowest of the three. The chunk closes with the tale of Locke study: lives and letters drawn from the Shaftesbury papers and great libraries.
caesar-commentaries-mcdevitte-bohn:
Julius Caesar wrote his own campaign reports in crisp third-person Latin. W. A. McDevitte's English translation covers the Gallic War and the Civil War. Caesar presents conquest as orderly, necessary, and brilliantly led.

The Gallic War's seven books trace campaigns across Gaul year by year. The Civil War books then follow his fight against Pompey and the Senate. Caesar's style is famous for clarity, speed, and cold control. Generations of students learned Latin from these pages. Read closely, they also show a master politician shaping his own legend in real time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-saint:
Ambrose Saint John, Oratorian born in 1815, died at Edgbaston, Birmingham, on 24 May 1875, son of Henry St. John of the Barons St. John of Bletsoe. Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, gave him his M.A. and his lifelong friendship with Newman. Curate to Henry Wilberforce at Walmer and East Farleigh, he joined Newman at Littlemore and entered the Church about a month before Newman's October 1845 conversion.

After Maryvale he accompanied Newman to Rome for priestly ordination, then began Birmingham mission work as Oratorians in 1847, moving to Edgbaston in 1852. There he laboured zealously in the Oratory and its famous school, a fine classical scholar and remarkable linguist in Oriental and European tongues. Overwork translating Fessler on infallibility during Newman's Gladstone discussion caused his death, and Newman's Apologia tribute endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-of-s:
The Epistles of Saint John are three canonical books of the New Testament by the Apostle John. For the First Epistle the entry weighs authenticity, canonicity, integrity, author, time and place, and purpose, then turns briefly to the Second and Third. The First Epistle is short, a hundred and five verses in five chapters, and its lateness might suggest no trace in the Apostolic Fathers, yet traces exist.

Polycarp, writing to the Philippians about 110 to 117, says that whoever denies Jesus Christ come in the flesh is Antichrist, an evident echo of First John chapter four. Harnack deems that witness conclusive proof that the First Epistle, and therefore John's Gospel, were written toward the end of Trajan's reign. Polycarp names neither John nor quotes word for word, since the Fathers cited from memory. The phrase come in the flesh also appears in Barnabas about 130.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-sai:
The Gospel of Saint John is the last of the four canonical Gospels in the traditional order. Ancient copies sometimes placed it after or even before Matthew. It narrates the life of Jesus from his baptism to his Resurrection and manifestation among his disciples. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its contents, peculiarities, authorship, composition, text, genuineness, and importance.

The Gospel falls into a prologue on the Incarnation of the Eternal Word and a first part on the public life to the eve of the Passion. A second part covers the Passion and Resurrection, with a short epilogue on the unrecorded words and works. The author follows historical order with special care for exact time and connection, chronicling the opening ministry almost like a diary, with four successive time marks at the start.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ida-hahn-hahn:
Ida Hahn-Hahn was a countess, convert, and authoress, born in 1805 and dead in 1880. She descended from one of Mecklenburg's wealthiest and most illustrious noble families. But her father, the famous theatrical count, squandered huge sums on drama, reduced the family to straits, and had to be placed under a guardian. Her pious mother's influence likewise repelled her.

The sixteen-year-old girl, due to prepare for confirmation, received a particularly superficial religious upbringing by her own admission. Her general education was just as deficient, leaving gaps she later filled by reading. At twenty-one she married her cousin Friedrich von Hahn, hereditary marshal of Basedow, hence her double name. It was a marriage of convenience, and the entry follows her path from society life to conversion and authorship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-von-:
Johannes von Kuhn was a speculative theologian of the Catholic school at Tubingen, ranked with Staudenmaier as its foremost dogmatist. Born in Wurttemberg in 1806, he studied at Tubingen and was ordained in 1831. He taught New Testament exegesis at Giessen. He moved to Tubingen in 1837, took the chair of dogmatic teaching in 1839, and retired in 1882.

His early work explored the thought of Jacobi. It opposed the destructive tendencies of Strauss in an unfinished Life of Jesus of 1838. His life's work, the Catholic Dogmatics, appeared only in parts. They were an introduction, a treatise on the knowledge, attributes, and unity of God, and a volume on the Trinity. Though never completed, it showed a clear thinker of remarkable gifts for philosophical theology, and his essays in the Tubingen journal carried his influence through the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prester-john:
Prester John names a legendary Eastern priest-king. A fabled 1122 Rome trip by a Patriarch John of India, with a visit to Callistus II, cannot be the legend's source.  Prester John's first sound mention stands in Otto of Freising's Chronicle, dated 1145.

Otto's source was Hugo, Bishop of Gabala, sent by Raymond of Antioch in 1144 to Pope Eugene III to seek help for Jerusalem. At Viterbo Otto met the Syrian prelate, and there, before the pope, he learned of a John who ruled the Far East as both priest and king. He had with his people turned Nestorian. A few years earlier John had beaten the monarchs of Media and Persia in a three day battle ending in the taking of Ecbatana.  Later lore finds his germ in Jenghiz Khan, the Mongol conqueror who crushed Islam's power in Central Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cyrus-and:
Cyrus and John were martyrs of the Coptic Church. They earned the titles wonderworkers and silverless ones because they cured the sick for nothing. This entry draws mainly on the encomium by Sophronius of Jerusalem. Nothing is known of their birth or youth, and sources disagree over whether John came from Edessa or Alexandria.

Cyrus practised medicine at Alexandria and preached as he healed. Then he fled Diocletian's prefect to a coastal town in Egypt, where he took the monastic habit and lived as an ascetic. John, a high-ranking soldier, sought him out, and the two were later martyred together. Three Roman churches once bore their names, and their feast is 31 January.
doe-osti-2573396-instantaneous-waveform-: Catching grid voltage flickers in real time got its DOE tech, and this report covers the waveform meters. The pages detail the gadgets. The grid engineers get their eyes. The eyes were instant. The gadgets were detailed. The meters were waveform.
doe-osti-3023219-frameworks-algorithms-a: FASTMath got frameworked, and this DOE SciDAC institute covers scalable math. The pages detail the technology findings. The computing folks get their data. The technologies were scalable. The data were computing. The institute was SciDAC. The math were frameworks. The technologies were scalable.
doe-osti-3029711-frameworks-algorithms-a: Math researchers getting their scalable toolkit wrapped up got the DOE FASTMath finale, and this final covers the institute. The pages detail the results. The computing folks get their closeout. The finale was technical. The toolkit were scalable. The researchers were math.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CisnerosRogelio: FBI Name Search Request Form: the bureau's Form 422 routed through the Name Searching Unit and Special File Room - the Rogelio Cisneros request. The bureaucracy's paper trail, complete. A US government document from the archive. Readers will find it rewarding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeLoreanJohn_De: A Newsday article dated July 27, 1987 covers a deposition involving car maker John DeLorean and the aging of documents. The piece reports on sworn testimony about how old certain documents really were, a question that turned on tests and expert judgment. The surviving record gives the article's paper, date, and subject, but not its detailed findings, so it stands as a dated news report on that legal fight.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GeorgeJohn_Geor:
An Associated Press report describes an unlikely rescue at sea. The U.S. Coast Guard and two Cuban patrol boats cooperated to save seven Americans from a grounded boat off Cuba. The rescue happened on Christmas, with the two Cold War rivals working the same water for the same crew.

Enemy services rarely share a mission, which is why the wire carried the story. For a few hours, seamanship outranked politics off the Cuban coast. The report preserves that brief cooperation in spare wire-service form, a small human footnote to a hostile decade.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinoJohn_Mar:
An FBI memorandum from Miami, dated May 8, 1964, is captioned 'Lee Harvey Oswald — Internal Security — Cuba.' It refers back to a report by Special Agent James J. O'Connor, dated April 4, 1964. O'Connor's subject was John V. Martino of Miami Beach. Martino was an anti-Castro activist whose name runs through the exile politics of those years.

The memo is a link in a chain: one agent's report on an exile figure, folded into the Oswald file by another office. Such cross-references show how the bureau organized a case with thousands of names. A reader can follow the paper from Martino, to O'Connor, to the file where the bureau kept its Oswald material.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SparrowJohn_Spa: Harold Weisberg, one of the earliest critics of the Warren Commission, wrote a direct reply to John Sparrow. Sparrow had criticized the writing of Weisberg and of Mark Lane, another leading Warren Commission critic. Weisberg answers back and defends their work. The short piece captures the sharp public fights that broke out in the late 1960s between assassination researchers and their reviewers.
historical-papers-part-3-from-volume-vi-:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote these historical papers, drawn from the sixth volume of his works. Whittier, the Quaker poet, writes here as an essayist of old New England. The set opens with a defence of Daniel O'Connell, the Irish liberator. It answers a Senate speech by Henry Clay from 1839.

Other papers treat James the Second, the border war of 1708, and the great Ipswich fright. Boy captives, Black men in two wars, and the Scottish reformers follow. The Pilgrims, Governor Endicott, and John Winthrop close the list. Readers meet Whittier's moral, plain-spoken take on the colonial past he loved.
king-john:
King John, by William Shakespeare, opens as King John receives Chatillion, an envoy from France. Queen Elinor, Pembroke, Essex, and Salisbury enter with the King. Chatillion has come to speak for the King of France. John asks plainly what France would have with them now. Chatillion greets him, then questions his right to rule England.

Chatillion calls John's majesty borrowed, and Elinor repeats the phrase in surprise. John tells his mother to be silent and hear the embassy. Philip of France, Chatillion says, claims England for Arthur Plantagenet. Arthur is son of John's dead brother Geoffrey, the speech explains. That claim, laid to the island and its lands, drives the scene.
occasional-poems-part-3-from-volume-iv-o:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote the poems gathered here. They form part three of volume four of his works. Whittier was a well known American poet and abolitionist. The contents list hymns, songs, and poems for public events. Titles include Eva, A Song of Harvest, and Kenoza Lake.

Many poems mark places, seasons, and civic moments in New England. Others honor friends, churches, and national anniversaries. Eva responds to the tale of Uncle Tom's Cabin. The hymns were sung at church openings and school closings. Together they show Whittier as a public, moral voice. Several pieces were written for named days and public gatherings.
personal-poems-i-part-1-from-volume-iv-o: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems I, the title page and contents of part 1 of volume 4 of Whittier's works, with no poems visible. The list begins with A Lament and poems to the memory of Charles B. Storrs and S. Oliver Torrey, then runs through Leggett's Monument, Chalkley Hall, tributes to Channing and Kossuth, and the celebrated Ichabod and The Lost Occasion.
personal-poems-ii-part-2-from-volume-iv-: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Personal Poems II, the title page, contents, and a poem heading, with no verse text visible. Part 2 of volume 4 of Whittier's works opens with The Cross and The Hero, then offers tributes to Rantoul, Charles Sumner, and Burns. Memorials of Joseph Sturge and Brown of Ossawatomie follow, and poems for Lydia Maria Child, Garibaldi, Bryant, and Bayard Taylor.
poems-in-wartime-part-4-from-volume-iii-:
John Greenleaf Whittier, the Quaker poet of Massachusetts, speaks in this volume as America's conscience during the Civil War. The contents gather his In War Time group, poems written as the conflict burned: To John C. Fremont, the Watchers, the Battle Autumn of 1862, and At Port Royal, alongside the famous Barbara Frietchie, the story of an old woman defying Confederate troops with a Union flag.

Whittier had been an abolitionist editor before he was a war poet, and the anti-slavery fire runs through the collection. A hymn for the celebration of emancipation, the Proclamation, and pieces on St. Helena Island, where freed people were building new lives. A dedication to his old friends Samuel and Harriet Sewall recalls that these lines stood at the front of the original volume. The poems read as a diary of the Union cause in verse.
prester-john:
John Buchan dedicated Prester John to Lionel Phillips in a poem of farewell to youth. Time, he writes, must capture the best of us. Travel and battle and gems and gold can no longer kindle the ancient rapture. Yet in Phillips, he thinks, the boy is not over. So he offers this medley of ways and wars. It comes from a fellow-lover of the fairest country under the stars.

The country is South Africa. The medley is Buchan's first great adventure novel. Its narrator is Davie Crawfurd, a Scots storekeeper's assistant. Contents promise the man on the Kirkcaple shore, where Davie first sees a strange preacher. Then come fortune, the winter veld, and Mr. Wardlaw's premonition. Behind them waits John Laputa, raising a rising under Prester John's banner. A fortune in gold waits too. Few thrillers have ever matched its pace.
reminiscent-poems-part-3-from-volume-ii-:
John Greenleaf Whittier grouped these poems as subjective and reminiscent, in a third part drawn from his works. The contents list opens with Memories and Raphael, then turns personal: To My Sister, My Thanks, My Namesake, and My Psalm. The Barefoot Boy, his famed poem of boyhood, stands among them.

The first poem, Memories, begins with a beautiful, happy girl, her step as light as summer air. Her mind unfolds leaf by leaf like a morning flower, and her heart wakes like a fine-toned lute at every breath of feeling. Forgiveness, Remembrance, A Memory, My Dream, and The Waiting complete a set steeped in family, loss, and faith.
tales-and-sketches-part-3-from-volume-v-:
Tales and Sketches by John Greenleaf Whittier collects the poet's prose, drawn here from the fifth volume of his works. The contents open with The Little Iron Soldier, or What Aminadab Ivison Dreamed About, and range across New England history, folklore, and factory life.

Passaconaway tells of the great Penacook sachem; The Opium Eater and The Proselytes follow; then come David Matson, The Fish I Didn't Catch, Yankee Gypsies, and The Training. Patucket Falls and First Day in Lowell bring in the mill towns, and Charms and Fairy Faith and Magicians and Witch Folk gather the old superstitions. The first tale opens at one in the morning. Aminadab Ivison starts up in bed. He has had a tried night of kicking and threshing. He wakes to tell his wife his dream.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-43-joh:
John in King James translation, starts with the Word, who was with God and was God in the beginning. All things were made by him, the first verses say, and without him nothing made was made.

In him was life, and that life was the light of men, shining in darkness the darkness did not grasp. A man sent from God, named John, came to bear witness to that light, though he was not the light himself. The true light, the text says, lights every man coming into the world. He was in the world he made, yet the world did not know him.
the-lady-of-fort-st-john: Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this novel of old Acadia in 1891. She had written The Romance of Dollard before it. She dedicated the book to two Acadians of the present day. Dr. John-George Bourinot of Ottawa and Dr. George Stewart of Quebec are they. Both were natives of Nova Scotia. Only the title page, dedication, and preface's first line are present here. The story itself does not appear. The preface asks how we can care for shadows when we may go back through the past itself.
the-splendid-spur-being-memoirs-of-the-a:
Arthur T. Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, presents the memoirs of John Marvel. Marvel served King Charles I in the civil war years 1642 and 1643. He wrote the memoirs himself. The editor has put them into modern English. A dedication letter to Edward Gwynne Eardley-Wilmot, dated from Torquay in August 1889, explains that under Jack Marvel's coat beats the heart of the author's friend.

An introductory note then untangles a curiosity of the time: three writers were using the popular signature Q, and none would surrender the letter. The public, Quiller-Couch says, had to decide which of them was Q to it, and readers of this 1897 edition meet the claimant whose historical adventure follows.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-john:
Book sixty-two in the World English Bible is the first letter of John. Its opening speaks of what existed from the beginning. The writer stresses what was heard, seen, and touched. That testimony concerns the Word of life. Eternal life, once with the Father, has now been revealed.

The letter announces a simple message: God is light. No darkness exists in him at all. Walking in darkness while claiming fellowship is called a lie. Walking in light brings fellowship and cleansing from sin. Claiming to have no sin, John warns, is self-deception. Readers receive a short, searching letter on honesty, light, and forgiveness.
the-world-english-bible-web-john:
John's Gospel, book forty-three in the World English Bible, begins with the Word. The Word was with God in the beginning, and was God. All things were made through him. Life in him becomes light for humanity. That light shines in darkness, which cannot overcome it. A footnote explains the Greek word can also mean comprehend.

John the baptizer then enters as a witness. He is not the light himself, the Gospel stresses. He testifies so that all might believe. The true light was coming into the world. Readers meet a Gospel unlike the other three. Theology and narrative intertwine from its first soaring lines.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
First John appears here in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech rendering, third edition, 1913. It is book 62 in his New Testament set. The letter opens with a claim to have seen and touched the Word of Life. That life, the writer says, was shown to the world and can now be shared.

The early verses give the core claim that God is light, with no darkness in him at all. Those who walk in the light share life with each other. Confessed sin, the letter adds, meets a faithful God who forgives. Weymouth's plain words keep the short letter easy to read aloud.

Second John is book 63 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The writer calls himself the Elder and writes to a chosen lady and her children. He rejoices that some of her children live true lives. His one old command is that they love one another.

Love, he says, means living by God's commands. He warns that many who deny Christ in the flesh have gone out into the world. Such teachers should not be housed or greeted. The letter is short, and it ends with hope of a face to face talk. Weymouth keeps its brief charge in plain, warm words.

Third John, book 64 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech set, third edition, 1913, is a brief note from the Elder to his friend Gaius. The writer prays that Gaius may thrive and stay well in body as he does in soul. Visiting brothers have praised the man's faith and his open house.

Trouble comes from Diotrephes, who loves first place and blocks guests from the church. The Elder vows to face his conduct when he comes. By contrast, Demetrius wins praise from all. Weymouth gives the tiny letter in fresh, direct words. Readers see early church friendship, welcome, and pride in a few short verses.

John's Gospel is book 43 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The first line speaks of the Word, who was with God and was God. All things came to be through him, and life in him was light for men. That light shines in the dark, and the dark has not won.

John the witness then enters, sent to point men to the light. The Word came to his own world, yet his own people gave him no welcome. Those who did trust gained the right to be God's children. Weymouth's clear opening lines keep the deep thought easy to grasp.
